name: Acetyl tetrapeptide-2

lead: Acetyl tetrapeptide-2 is a short synthetic peptide (acetyl-Lys-Asp-Val-Tyr) used in skin-firming and anti-aging cosmetics, sold under names such as Thymulen 4, and it appears in some hair lotions. People use it for firmer, tighter, younger-looking skin.

Suppliers say it mimics thymopoietin, a thymus hormone, and prompts keratinocytes to release GM-CSF, activating skin Langerhans cells and supporting epidermal regeneration. A 2018 cell study found it changed stiffness and gene expression (COL17A1) in cultured keratinocytes, and a 2021 randomized study tested a hair lotion combining it with creatine and B vitamins. No trial has tested it alone on facial wrinkles or firmness.

paras: It is applied in daily creams and serums for firmness, or in scalp and hair lotions combined with other ingredients. Visible changes from such products are generally judged over weeks to months.
No safety data were found beyond its status as a cosmetic ingredient, and the supporting claims are largely manufacturer-reported.

angle.text: Acetyl tetrapeptide-2 (Thymulen 4) is marketed in skin-firming and anti-aging products to support epidermal regeneration for firmer, tighter skin. Support comes from cell-culture data and one combination-lotion hair study.

lead: Acetyl tetrapeptide-2 is a synthetic four-amino-acid peptide (acetyl-Lys-Asp-Val-Tyr) used in skin-firming and anti-aging cosmetics and in some hair lotions, sold by suppliers under names such as Thymulen 4.[1] It is aimed at making skin look firmer and more youthful, and at supporting the look of fuller hair in lotions where it is combined with other actives.[1][2]

It is described as mimicking thymopoietin, a thymus hormone, and is claimed to counter the age-related decline of thymic factors and to support skin immune defences and epidermal regeneration.[1] A 2018 cell study found that the peptide changed the stiffness and gene expression of cultured keratinocytes.[3]

In a 2021 randomized controlled study of 100 women with acute telogen effluvium, a lotion combining the peptide with creatine and B vitamins was reported by the authors to appear to accelerate recovery from the condition, with higher anagen-to-telogen ratios at weeks 4 and 8 than the shampoo-only group.[2][4] No trial has tested the peptide alone on facial wrinkles or firmness.

paras: Supplier-derived descriptions say the peptide stimulates keratinocytes to produce GM-CSF, which promotes maturation of Langerhans cells and thereby raises skin immune surveillance.[1] Such descriptions are manufacturer claims and have not been independently tested in published trials.

A 2021 open, randomized controlled study (Turlier and colleagues) in 100 women aged 19 to 50 with acute telogen effluvium compared a lotion containing creatine, acetyl tetrapeptide-2 and B vitamins plus a mild shampoo (51 women) with the mild shampoo alone (49 women). Both groups had a higher anagen-to-telogen ratio at week 16 than at baseline. The lotion group showed significantly higher ratios at weeks 4 and 8, a significant fall in telogen hair density at all time points, and investigator-rated improvement in hair density, and the lotion was well tolerated.[2][4] Because the lotion combined several actives and the control was shampoo alone, the results cannot be attributed to the peptide by itself.
No studies were found of acetyl tetrapeptide-2 as a single ingredient in facial skin.

In immortalized human keratinocytes (HaCaT), atomic force microscopy showed that the peptide raised cell stiffness after 48 hours, most notably at a low concentration, and it increased expression of the COL17A1 gene.[3] This was an in vitro study, not a test on living skin.
The peptide is marketed in serums, creams and masks.[1] No looksmaxxing community discussion was identified.

timeline.event: A cell study reports effects of the peptide on keratinocyte stiffness and COL17A1 expression.[3]
Randomized study of a multi-ingredient lotion containing the peptide in women with acute telogen effluvium is published.[2]
